claims.text: The as-cast high-entropy alloy has a largely random distribution of constituent elements and high chemical disorder.
The as-cast alloy currently shows no clear superconducting transition at low temperatures.
Moderate post-solidification annealing will promote short-range chemical ordering without causing full phase segregation.
Annealing-induced short-range ordering reduces electron-scattering centers.
Disordered atomic clusters and grain-boundary irregularities act as electron-scattering centers in this alloy.
The proposed annealing treatment preserves the overall high-entropy state.
Reducing the density of scattering centers reduces superconducting pair-breaking effects.
Reduced scattering increases the effectiveness of electron-phonon interactions.
More effective electron-phonon interactions enable Cooper-pair formation through a conventional BCS mechanism.
Annealed samples will exhibit a superconducting transition relative to the as-cast baseline.
The annealed samples will have a higher critical temperature than the as-cast samples.
The predicted superconducting transition will produce a resistivity drop and a diamagnetic signal.
Excessive electron scattering from random atomic arrangements prevents a robust superconducting transition in the as-cast state.
The hypothesis should hold only when annealing remains below roughly 0.5 times the alloy melting temperature and avoids full phase segregation.
Annealing beyond the proposed thermal window may disrupt the alloy's high-entropy character.
Disruption of the high-entropy state may cause different superconducting or non-superconducting behavior or detrimental mechanical properties.
The exact critical-temperature shift and the amount of ordering required are composition-dependent and presently uncertain.
